text: @Slai.  Yeah, I got the XFX 8gb variant, it'll get most modern games to about 58 fps with highest possible settings. Sea of Thieves seems to bounce between 40 and 110 fps, though. I think it's a good card, but I can't help but feel like I need a bit more power to have a more steady and stable framerate. But coming from a 5450, by the gods, it's 1000x better than that. text: @GangsterDolphins I have A6 7400K and it's really weak CPU. It barely cuts it for HTPC purposes and light emulation. It lags at Youtube 1080p60fps videos. I have tried using it for lower demanding games and older games, neither offered exactly perfect performance, the best it can is to play UT2004 at max settings at 1080p and gets around 60fps average and Far Cry at 1080p maxed out, but then fps is at 45-50 at average. The best it can emulate is PS1. PS2 emulation on it is hit or miss, some games work fine at full speed, but others run like garbage. In general usage it's not great either, it often lags or slows down. It's based on bulldozer architecture and if anything, it was suited for many cores. It was weak per core, but at least if you had many cores it wasn't too bad. I have Athlon X4 845 in another PC and it's much faster CPU and actually is usable. Arguably it's better than FX 6300 as it has the last alteration of bulldozer deprived architecture, which is the most fixed one. I own quite a bit of dozer CPUs, but I would say to avoid dual cores. They aren't even true dual cores either, more like over engineered single core CPU with stronger than hyper threading multicore performance. In other words at this time they are complete crap. A GPU may help with gaming, but it will be just bottlenecked. The only thing it's good at would be if you wanted to build computer for older games, with goal to aim at around similar performance of old Core 2 Duo, then it's something.

text:
Hey Linus! I made a liquid cooling system for my laptop in possibly the jankiest way ever. I think you should do it again, but better than I did.

Instead of finding some way to make a liquid cooling block for the hot components, I just built an adapter with heatpipes that gives me a handy copper plate out the back of my laptop to which I (currently clamped) bolted a Corsair H200. My setup keeps everything under 85C no problem, and it has several major issues (suboptimal heat pipe contact, bad bending, lots of deformation). You can get 70 watt heatpipes on Digikey for like $5 apiece, I ripped apart some laptop coolers and desoldered the CPU contact plates to get my copper plates, make sure you check the datasheet when you order the heatpipes, obey the minimum bend radius, and order twice as many heatpipes as you think you need.

I can provide pics if there's interest.

text:
Average framerates to be honest are not that accurate about a PC's performance. You can clearly see how the dominated RX 580 magically pummels the GTX 1070 in GTA 5! How even is this possible. In any means, a 1070 is a dinosaur compared to the RX 580 in ALL games I give you the word. Minimum framerates however, can somewhat determine how well or not-so-well a PC performs. So what can be used to compare GPU's?
Frametimes! Yes. Frametimes are a very important factor in determining how consistent a GPU is at handling games and that it does NOT cause any stuttering, lag or drops. So, a PC that gives a consistent 60 fps is smoother than a pc that gives laggy 80 fps. Hence, frametimes show what is real! For a more elaborate explaination, you can see Bitwit's video titled "1% & 0.1% Lows Explained!" (No offense to Linus, I love him as much as Bitwit; no homo). 
If you've seen the video already, you know that LTT here mistakenly didn't show the right performances of the cards. I, personally prefer frametime as my main factor in determining a GPU's capacity. 
Anyway, thank you for reading (and possibly considering) my comment! [I have an RX 470 and I feel bad for my card :'(  In case you wondered].

I just find it odd how they used to market the RX480 as comparable with the GTX1060 yet now apparently it's the RX580 that is barely competing with it? Time to sell those AMD stocks unless you want to bet Vega is slightly better..

Here is where you are wrong with factual source provided: http://gpuboss.com/gpus/Radeon-RX-480-vs-GeForce-GTX-1060

The 480 had newer 14nm transitors (more expensive and even more of them) yet equaled performance of less 16nm transistors, compute units, etc.. The RX480 still had lower clockspeed, pixel rate, etc.. and performance was basically tied with a GTX 1060 even with all that added memory, compute units, and other components: the main factor which made the GTX 1060 win was the power consumption (30 less W of power needed), heat, and noise factors. It's obvious that the GTX1060 is factually 'doing more' with 'less'.

'Dumbed down' 1060GTX isn't even a top of the line NVidia card; it's a performance medium between lowest and top at the ~200$ range for those who want a powerful upgrade.

The 480 lost in everything other than being about equalized in performance on all applications. 

All the other shit about DX12 when less than 1% of games use those APIs (maybe 1% in a few years?) is just a marketing flop because you'll be getting "best" value by getting the card that runs better in OpenGL1-4x, DX8,DX9,DX10,DX11, which consists of the other 99% of games or rendering apps you will be running. 

You're basically a total moron if you're going to reply talking about something like Vulkan or magical drivers that alter your hardware effect because NVidia cards gain the same performance increases on Vulkan/DX12 and overall both get excessively more frames than you would even need. It's a generic 'programming' optimization, not a magical 1 company bias. The logic is like saying "when we use a blackhole to create energy, we'll be the real winners!" but you're basically a moron and you are just justifying getting something slightly worse for the same price; when both are good but one is just factually better. 

If you are really a freak you wouldn't be spending for the cost-efficient best upgrade but rather just getting the 1000$ one and whining about it. If you spent 200$ on a GPU recently then I am sure it will last many years unless something else is holding it back.

text:
The rx480 can be had for a lot cheaper. It goes on sale and rebate more often in my experience. It has higher power consumption, but for some $20 or $40 less, you can have an rx480 which is neck and neck if not beating out the gtx 1060 in some titles (just look at the benchmarks in this video). Drivers can have a huge effect on GPUs. I don't know why you discount that. DX12 likely won't be the standard for another 2 or 3 years, but it's coming, and you'd have to have memory loss not to understand that. Look at DX9, 10, 11.

One other thing that I'd argue is a pretty big deal. RX480s support crossfire while gtx 1060s don't support SLI. RX480s in crossfire perform about on par with a gtx 1080 despite crossfire scaling, and the performance scaling at 1440p and 4k is slightly better on polaris compared to pascal, meaning that you could conceivably throw another rx480 in your machine whenever you want in the next few months or year for under $400 and have something equivalent to a 1080.

text: Lol at the OP. I bought an RX480 for my studio build back in December and for the next 3 months I thought my motherboard was dying..... Why wasn't I smart enough to realize it was just the piece of shit GPU I just slapped on my mobo? Idk, probably because of idiots like OM9H4X who fail to report accurately on the 480. After putting this horrific excuse for a GPU in my build, I was experiencing constantly BSOD's, red screen restarts, black screen shut downs, not to mention all of the bugs in video games (weird reflection bugs with AA enabled) , driver problems, overheating issues, and wattman errors that caused my games to crash (even though I never overclocked the damn card). After swapping the psu, the constant shut downs (still) led me to believe my motherboard was leaving me .... Snif...Snif...However, after researching the overheating problems I was experiencing with my 480, (and no it wasn't early adoption overheating, this was as recent as a month ago) I started to realize I wasn't the only one experiencing all of these issues. In fact, if you look on NewEgg, there's not a singe RX480 from AMD, or any of their partners listed that have a 5 egg review. Now, I know newegg egg count is hardly a test of quality. However, the point I'm trying to make is, when you read the reviews, you start to realize there's a trend taking place among 480 users. And they reflected the problems I was having exactly. So, you guessed it..... I took the damn thing out of my build , replaced it with an MSI GTX1060, and wala....... Problems gone. Not only that, but whatta you know, you can actually overclock a 1060. It doesn't thermal throttle (ALWAYS) , it doesn't give me bugs in games with MSAA turned on like the 480 did, it doesn't really do anything. In fact, the 1060 is quite boring. It just...... works. So yeah, I'd say the 1060 overshadowed the 480. And so would any realistic tech enthusiast. You're just a crazed brand worshiping maniac. And you can't say the same thing to me because I bought the 480 first. That was the card I wanted. It just, failed me. Why didn't the tech review sites pick up on all of these problems associated with the 480? Well, to put it short , because they do test bench reviews. They aren't using the 480 for a month and then reporting back to us. They're throwing the damn thing on a test bench for an hour, running some synthetic benchmarks and games and posting the FPS. It's hardly an accurate account of reality. I'm taking a break from AMD for a little while.... I think they're in over their head at the moment and have entirely too much on their plate (not that I'm complaining). However, It's resulting in very very poor driver support and just an overall bad experience for some consumers.

text:
That's exactly what I'm talking about then. AMD will never have a card that competes with nVidia at the top end. It's the same with AMD v. Intel in the CPU category. AMD's products are great for lower budgets. Yes nVidia offers products at the same price points, but on a budget, every dollar matters. I can also imagine that on a tight budget, the differences in performance are not something that would be earth shattering if picking either brand. 

I guess the real difference is that if you care about budget, buy whatever is the cheapest. There are only two players here, it's not like you will end up buying a product that is an off-brand ripoff or a poorly build imitation brand that lowers its price by cutting corners. Both companies are reputable and have been in the game for a very long time. So I guess my confusion in the argument is that all the people praising nVidia talk about the 1080ti and get insulted by the people praising AMD. There is no argument. the 1080ti is better than anything AMD has. It's not a matter of opinion, it's fact. It's very doubtful AMD will ever have a flagship card that outperforms nVidia's flagship card. There is a possibility, but it's unlikely based on their track record.

 I'm just honestly sick of people trying to claim that people that buy nVidia products are "fanboys". Typically the people buying nVidia cards are not interested in price to performance, they just want the best card money can buy. and that "best" status is not by a small margin. As for people who buy 1060s or 1050s, I'm not really sure. I can imagine, though, since AMD's flagship cards are priced similarly to nVidia's budget cards that buying AMD would be more beneficial since those cards would come with more extras and such.
